concept.name: Bull flattener
concept.definition: A flattening of the yield curve driven by long-term interest rates falling faster than short-term rates. It is called 'bull' because falling yields mean rising bond prices, and the pattern often appears in flight-to-safety episodes or when inflation expectations decline.
concept.intuition: The curve flattens from the long end rallying: long rates drop faster than short rates.
concept.mechanics: Classified by decomposing the spread change: the back-end yield falls faster than the front-end yield, narrowing the spread. A flattener position (short front leg, long back leg) gains; the long back leg, with its high duration, captures most of the rally.
concept.formula: Condition: Δy_long < 0 and Δ(y_long - y_short) < 0, i.e. the back-end yield falls faster than the front-end yield.
concept.failure_modes: Descriptive, not predictive: bull flatteners often occur late in tightening cycles and can reverse if the short end suddenly re-prices. Because the long leg dominates the P&L, a flattener during a bull flattener is effectively a large duration bet, with corresponding mark-to-market volatility.
concept.misconceptions: A bull flattener is not 'good news for borrowers' in a simple sense — it frequently signals recession risk (long yields falling on growth fears while the policy rate stays high). It also does not mean short rates cannot fall at all; they simply fall less.
concept.example: The 10-year yield drops from 4.5% to 3.9% on a growth scare while the 2-year holds near 4.9%; the 2s10s spread narrows from -40 bp to -100 bp — a bull flattener.

citations.source: LearnBonds: Bull Flattener, Bear Flattener, Bull Steepener and Bear Steepener Explained
